whatItIs.text: The laid egg of a bird — for most kitchens the chicken's — and one of cooking's most versatile ingredients, binding, leavening, thickening, and enriching.

historyNote.text: Chickens were likely domesticated for their eggs before 7500 BC from junglefowl of Southeast Asia, and people there were harvesting eggs by 1500 BC; the egg carton arrived much later, invented in 1911 in British Columbia to settle a dispute about broken eggs.

howToChoose.text: Check the date and open the box; freshness floats downward in water but the simplest test is the pack date — buy the coldest-boxed, most recent stock.

storage.text: Keep eggs in the box in the main body of the fridge, not the door. The rulebook has the storage window and raw-egg cautions.
storage.note: egg storage and raw-egg guidance live in the food-safety rulebook

useItUp.text: Eggs approaching their date are ideal for baking, hard-boiling, or a straight-up omelette; one egg plus breadcrumbs rescues almost any leftover mash into patties.

substitutions.note: as a binder in bakes; no leavening, rest 10 minutes to gel
